Hello! 

I wanted to know more about output of the higher order using the summary() and inspect(). 
If I were create a normal CFA, the latent covariance matrix is below. The summary() and inspect() are identical results. 

Covariances:
                        Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
  Factor1 ~~                                                            
    Factor2           0.423    0.070    6.028    0.000    0.813    0.813
  Factor2 ~~                                                            
    Factor3           0.232    0.045    5.148    0.000    0.785    0.785
  Factor1 ~~                                                            
    Factor3           0.349    0.049    7.072    0.000    0.692    0.692


> inspect(fit.first, what='cov.lv')
            Factr1 Factr2 Factr3
Factor1 0.885               
Factor2 0.423  0.306        
Factor3 0.349  0.232  0.287 


This looks great, and I create a higher order factor model. 
It looks fine from the output. 

 Higher order =~                                                           
    Factor1           1.000                                 0.732    0.732

    Factor3           0.728       NA                      0.936    0.936

But when I look at the output of the model using the summary().
This isn't what I expect. 

Covariances:
                         Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
Factor1 ~~                                                            
    Factor2           0.076    0.066    1.141    0.254    0.519    0.519
  Factor2 ~~                                                            
    Factor3          -0.020    0.020   -1.043    0.297   -0.476   -0.476
  Factor1 ~~                                                            
    Factor3           0.003    0.051    0.066    0.947    0.028    0.028

And oddly enough, if I use inspect(), the result is the same as the CFA model instead of the higher order CFA. 

> inspect(fit, what='cor.lv')
             Factr1 Factr2 Factr3 Parano
Factor1  1.000                      
Factor2  0.813  1.000               
Factor3  0.692  0.785  1.000        
Paranoia 0.732  0.912  0.936  1.000 

> inspect(fit, what='cov.lv')
             Factr1 Factr2 Factr3 Parano
Factor1  0.885                      
Factor2  0.423  0.306               
Factor3  0.349  0.232  0.287        
Paranoia 0.475  0.348  0.345  0.475 

So my question is why is the output from the summary() that shows the latent covariance different from the inspect()? 
And also, why is the covariance estimates of the covariance so bad when I use a higher order cfa? 

Thank you!
Aiden

messages.subject: Re: higher order
parts:
Aidan--
     All is not well. The "covariances" you see in the higehr order model are residual covariances, not total covariances. As free parameters, they make your higher order model not identified, which is why you have "NA"s for the standard errors of the loadings of the first order factors on the second order factor. The correation matrix you get from Inspect shows the toal correlations, not the residual correlations.
     You should fix the covariances among first order factors to 0 and re-estimate the model. When you do, you will find that its chi-square fit is identical to the fit of the model without the higher order factor.

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: higher order
parts:
Aidan--
     This is factor-based SEM 101. The factor model implies a covariance matrix for the observed variables, where each element of that matrix is a function of model parameters. Estimating those parameters means, in effect, solving for them out of that model-implied covariance matrix, using the elements of the sample-based covariance matrix as "knowns" to assign values to the "unknowns," the free model parameters. You can only solve for a certain parameter out of certain elements of the model-implied covariance matrix, because each parameter only appears in the formula for certain elements. You effectively consume elements once you use them to solve for one parameter--you can't use the same information over and over again to solve for parameter after parameter.
     With a higehr order factor model, you must think a little differently. Now you are solving out of the covariance matrix of the factors. The parameters for the higher order factor model--both the loadings of firt order factor and second order factor,m and the residual variances and covariances of the first order factors--are solved out of the covariance matrix of the factors. With three factors, there are only 3 ( 3-1) / 2 = 6 elements of the factor covariance matrix. That is the most parameters that you can estimate. With NO free residual covariances among the factors, you consume all 6 elements of this matrix. As soon as you try to estimate one residual covariance, your model is not identified. A model with three freely covarying factors involves the same number of free parameters--that is why this higehr order model and the freely covarying factor model are equivalent.

Edward, 

Okay. With higher order models you are effectively calculating DFs separately for the observed covariance matrix and the factor covariance matrix. So in instances like this, a higher order model with only two latent factors and one higher order factor should not work because you have 2(2+1)/2 = 3 known parameters, but you need to estimate 2 factor loadings, and 2 factor residuals, which would result in a negative df (3-4 = -1). Unless you fix to factor residuals or to factor loadings to zero, which would than just be a regular CFA.

On Wed, Oct 4, 2017 at 11:34 AM, Aiden <aide...@gmail.com> wrote:

Edward, 

Okay. With higher order models you are effectively calculating DFs separately for the observed covariance matrix and the factor covariance matrix. So in instances like this, a higher order model with only two latent factors and one higher order factor should not work because you have 2(2+1)/2 = 3 known parameters, but you need to estimate 2 factor loadings, and 2 factor residuals, which would result in a negative df (3-4 = -1). Unless you fix to factor residuals or to factor loadings to zero, which would than just be a regular CFA. 

On Wednesday, October 4, 2017 at 10:49:00 AM UTC-4, Edward Rigdon wrote:
Aidan--
     This is factor-based SEM 101. The factor model implies a covariance matrix for the observed variables, where each element of that matrix is a function of model parameters. Estimating those parameters means, in effect, solving for them out of that model-implied covariance matrix, using the elements of the sample-based covariance matrix as "knowns" to assign values to the "unknowns," the free model parameters. You can only solve for a certain parameter out of certain elements of the model-implied covariance matrix, because each parameter only appears in the formula for certain elements. You effectively consume elements once you use them to solve for one parameter--you can't use the same information over and over again to solve for parameter after parameter.
     With a higehr order factor model, you must think a little differently. Now you are solving out of the covariance matrix of the factors. The parameters for the higher order factor model--both the loadings of firt order factor and second order factor,m and the residual variances and covariances of the first order factors--are solved out of the covariance matrix of the factors. With three factors, there are only 3 ( 3-1) / 2 = 6 elements of the factor covariance matrix. That is the most parameters that you can estimate. With NO free residual covariances among the factors, you consume all 6 elements of this matrix. As soon as you try to estimate one residual covariance, your model is not identified. A model with three freely covarying factors involves the same number of free parameters--that is why this higehr order model and the freely covarying factor model are equivalent.

On Wed, Oct 4, 2017 at 7:01 AM, Aiden <aide...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thanks Edward. I didn't realise that the covariance section in the summary() refers to the residual and not the factor covariances.  

Why would it make my model unidentified when I include a single higher order factor? I would imagine that I only have 3 extra parameters to estimate. My DF is 165 for the CFA, and 162 for higher order. 




On Tuesday, October 3, 2017 at 4:38:29 PM UTC-4, Edward Rigdon wrote:
Aidan--
     All is not well. The "covariances" you see in the higehr order model are residual covariances, not total covariances. As free parameters, they make your higher order model not identified, which is why you have "NA"s for the standard errors of the loadings of the first order factors on the second order factor. The correation matrix you get from Inspect shows the toal correlations, not the residual correlations.
     You should fix the covariances among first order factors to 0 and re-estimate the model. When you do, you will find that its chi-square fit is identical to the fit of the model without the higher order factor.
